Akathisia is an inner restlessness that drives repetitive movement, and the
movement usually fails to relieve it. That failure is the part worth
explaining, and accounts pitched at the receptor do not on their own explain
it. I am building an active inference account alongside them, which asks
whether the disorder sits in how bodily prediction errors are turned into
action rather than in the motor system itself.

## The syndrome has two halves {.k-head}

Braude, Barnes and Gore put the clinical features through a principal components
analysis in 1983, working from consecutive psychiatric admissions, and the
features did not collapse onto one dimension. There is what the patient reports,
an inner restlessness that sitting still does not settle. There is what you see
from the other side of the desk, the weight shifting and the rocking. On the
ward the gap between the two is not subtle. You can watch someone's legs for a
minute and still have to ask.

Six years later Barnes built the rating scale around that split. Objective
movement gets its own items, subjective distress gets its own, and a global
judgement sits on top of both. Any scale carries an assumption about what it is
measuring, and this one assumes the halves are separate enough to score
separately.

It also names the case where they separate completely. Pseudoakathisia is the
movement with the complaint missing. Miller and Fleischhacker treat the
subjective and objective components as distinct throughout their review, and
their prevalence figures show what that costs: estimates run from 5 percent to
nearly 37 percent, depending on which half is being counted and how strictly.

A range that wide is mostly the definition talking. Which half you count, and
how strictly, moves the answer by a factor of seven. That is the part I keep
coming back to. A receptor account predicts a dose of movement disorder. It does
not say why the felt and the seen should be able to come apart at all.

## It did not go away with the newer drugs {.k-head}

Demyttenaere and colleagues pooled the trials of antipsychotics licensed more
recently and got a weighted incidence of 7.7 percent. That is lower than the
first-generation figures and it is not close to zero.

The treatment evidence is where it gets strange. Gerolymos and colleagues ran a
network meta-analysis of what actually works against antipsychotic-induced
akathisia, and the drugs that beat placebo were mirtazapine (SMD −1.20),
biperiden (−1.01), vitamin B6 (−0.92) and propranolol (−0.78). That is a
serotonergic drug, an anticholinergic, a vitamin cofactor and a beta blocker:
four targets, none of them D2. Pringsheim and colleagues land somewhere similar
in the Canadian guideline, where most of the advice is about reducing or
withdrawing the offending drug and then reaching for agents aimed elsewhere.

This is the point where it would be easy to overclaim, so let me be careful.
None of that refutes a dopaminergic account. The drug that causes akathisia is a
dopaminergic drug, and no amount of arguing about levels of description changes
it. What is left is a syndrome whose two halves come apart, whose reported
frequency depends on which half you count, and which responds to four drugs that
do four different things. The level of description is worth arguing about.
